section: Case 2: After the Surgery
statement: A 41-year-old woman has a 3 cm squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix, confined to the cervix, with no nodes on PET. She wants surgery.

statement: Q: What is her FIGO 2018 stage before surgery? A: IB2

statement: Q: Her surgeon plans a radical hysterectomy. Which trial showed that the minimally invasive (laparoscopic/robotic) approach had worse disease-free and overall survival than open surgery? A: LACC

statement: Sedlis criteria lead to pelvic RT: GOG 92 cut recurrence roughly in half. Chemo is added for Peters features (GOG 109).

section: Case 2: After the Surgery > step 5: Target
statement: Q: What does the target include, and how do you account for motion at simulation? A: The vaginal cuff and upper vagina, parametria, and pelvic nodes (common, external, and internal iliac, obturator, and presacral). Simulate with a full and an empty bladder to capture how much the cuff moves (an ITV).

statement: Q: What side effects of pelvic RT do you counsel her about? A: Acute: diarrhea and cramping, urinary frequency and burning, fatigue, and mild skin irritation. Late: vaginal dryness and stenosis (dilators), leg lymphedema (higher after node dissection plus RT), bowel or bladder injury, insufficiency fractures of the pelvis, and early menopause if the ovaries are in the field.

section: hn-imaging
statement: Depth of invasion - the single biggest driver of oral cavity T-stage - is a soft-tissue measurement, and MRI's soft-tissue contrast resolves it far better than CT.

section: hn-imaging
statement: PET/CT about 12 weeks after treatment. Active tumor is FDG-avid while scar usually is not, so a negative scan can spare the patient a neck dissection.

section: hn-imaging

section: hn-staging
statement: A patient's workup shows no evidence of disease outside the head and neck region. What M-stage is this?

section: hn-treatment
statement: Outside of a clinical trial, HPV-positive disease is still treated with the same intensity as HPV-negative disease. Substituting cetuximab for cisplatin produced worse survival, and dose de-escalation strategies have so far failed to show they're safe.

section: hn-treatment
statement: A patient asks why the plan is trying to keep dose low in the muscles at the back of the throat. Which structures are these, and what toxicity are they linked to?

section: hn-tnm

section: hn-tnm

section: hn-tnm

section: hn-tnm

section: hn-tnm
statement: Masticator space, pterygoid plates, skull base, or carotid encasement is T4b, generally unresectable.

section: hn-tnm

section: hn-tnm
statement: Contralateral or bilateral nodes, none over 6 cm = cN2 in p16+ disease.

section: hn-tnm
statement: p16-positive tonsil cancer, 4.5 cm. What is the T stage?

section: hn-tnm
statement: Bone (skull base, cervical vertebra, pterygoid structures, sinuses) = T3.

section: hn-tnm
statement: Any cranial nerve involvement or intracranial extension = T4.

section: hn-tnm
statement: Cord fixation = T3. Impaired (but not fixed) mobility would be T2.

section: Anatomy > Step 1: Where Is It? > Sphenoid Sinus / Skull Base
statement: Sits right on top of the nasopharynx. Tumor that erodes this bone is T3; through the foramina into the skull it reaches the cranial nerves (T4).

section: Anatomy > Step 1: Where Is It? > Nasal Cavity (Turbinates)
statement: In front of the nasopharynx. Tumor growing forward causes nasal obstruction and bloody discharge, but nasal cavity extension alone is still T1.

section: Anatomy > Step 1: Where Is It? > Oropharynx
statement: Directly below the nasopharynx. NPC that spreads down into the oropharynx is still T1.

section: Anatomy > Step 2: Zoomed In > Fossa of Rosenmüller
statement: Lateral recess behind the torus tubarius. The single most common site of origin of nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and the first place to look on MRI.

section: Anatomy > Step 2: Zoomed In > Eustachian Tube Orifice
statement: Opening just in front of the torus. Obstruction causes ear fullness and conductive hearing loss on one side.

section: Anatomy > Step 2: Zoomed In > Posterior Choanae
statement: Back of the nasal cavity, the anterior boundary of the nasopharynx. Tumor extending forward into the nasal cavity is still T1.

section: Anatomy > Step 2: Zoomed In > Posterosuperior Wall (Adenoids)
statement: Roof and back wall, lying against the sphenoid and clivus. Upward spread here reaches the skull base (T3).

section: Anatomy > Step 2: Zoomed In > Clivus / Skull Base
statement: Superior boundary. Bone invasion is T3; spread through the foramina to the cavernous sinus can affect CN III, IV, V, and VI (T4).

section: Anatomy > Step 2: Zoomed In > Soft Palate (Inferior Boundary)
statement: Floor of the nasopharynx and roof of the oropharynx. Extension below it into the oropharynx is still T1 in AJCC 8.

section: Anatomy > Axial / coronal MRI
statement: Axial / coronal MRI

section: Anatomy > Oral Cavity Subsites
statement: Midsagittal view of the head (face on the left). Buccal mucosa and retromolar trigone sit laterally, so they aren't visible on a midline cut.

section: Anatomy > Clinical photo: transoral view
statement: Tonsil and soft palate with the tonsillar pillars visible.

section: Anatomy > Axial MRI at the tonsil level

section: Anatomy
statement: Two of its four subsites, the tonsil and base of tongue, are where the HPV story of the last twenty years has played out.

section: Anatomy > Oropharynx Subsites > Base of Tongue

section: Case 1: The Spot on the Tongue > step 1: Exam
statement: Q: The patch is about 1 cm, does not scrape off with a tongue blade, and is not tender. There are no neck nodes. What is the best next step? A: Biopsy the lesion

section: Case 1: The Spot on the Tongue > step 1: Exam
statement: A white patch that does not wipe off (leukoplakia) or a red patch (erythroplakia) gets a biopsy, not reassurance.

section: Case 1: The Spot on the Tongue > step 2: Risk factors
statement: Q: Which of these is mainly a risk factor for a different head and neck subsite, not the oral cavity? A: High-risk HPV

section: Case 1: The Spot on the Tongue > step 2: Risk factors
statement: High-risk HPV drives oropharynx cancer (tonsil and base of tongue).

section: Case 1: The Spot on the Tongue > step 2: Risk factors
statement: Even a p16-positive oral tongue cancer is still staged as oral cavity, not oropharynx.

section: Case 1: The Spot on the Tongue > step 3: Biopsy
statement: Incisional biopsy: keratosis with severe epithelial dysplasia. No invasive carcinoma.

section: Case 1: The Spot on the Tongue > step 3: Biopsy
statement: Management is removal of the lesion when feasible, stopping tobacco and alcohol, and close surveillance with a re-biopsy of anything that changes.

section: Case 1: The Spot on the Tongue > step 4: Counseling
statement: That is why he stays in surveillance and why quitting smoking matters.

section: Case 2: The Raspy Voice > step 2: Scope
statement: Laryngoscopy showing a lesion on the left vocal cord. Crosetti E et al., Curr Oncol Rep 2024 (PMC11168980), CC BY 4.0.

section: Case 2: The Raspy Voice > step 2: Scope
statement: Flexible laryngoscopy: an irregular, exophytic lesion on the left true vocal cord that extends up onto the left false cord (supraglottis).

section: Case 2: The Raspy Voice > step 2: Scope
statement: Biopsy: invasive squamous cell carcinoma.

section: Case 2: The Raspy Voice > step 2: Scope
statement: CT neck: no cartilage invasion, no paraglottic space involvement, no enlarged nodes.

section: Case 2: The Raspy Voice > step 2: Scope
statement: A fixed cord (or paraglottic space or inner thyroid cartilage invasion) would make it T3.

section: Case 2: The Raspy Voice > step 3: Imaging
statement: Q: Which scan is the workhorse for staging laryngeal cancer, and why? A: CT, because cartilage invasion defines the T-stage and CT shows bone and cartilage best

section: Case 2: The Raspy Voice > step 3: Imaging
statement: MRI is better for soft tissue and perineural spread, and PET-CT for nodes and distant disease.

section: Case 2: The Raspy Voice > step 4: Treatment
statement: A total laryngectomy would be far too much for a T2 cancer with a working larynx.

section: Case 2: The Raspy Voice > step 5: Nodal levels
statement: Nodal risk is about 2% for T1 and 5% for T2 glottic cancer.

section: Case 2: The Raspy Voice > step 6: Counseling
statement: Q: He asks what to expect during treatment and whether he can do anything to improve his chances. What do you tell him? A: Expect a sore throat, a hoarse voice that often gets worse during treatment before it improves, redness of the skin on the front of the neck, and fatigue. Dry mouth is mild because the field is small. Stop smoking: smoking during RT worsens both tumor control and side effects.

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving > step 1: Exam
statement: A painless level II neck mass in a younger nonsmoker is the classic presentation of HPV-positive oropharynx cancer.

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving > step 2: Imaging
statement: Q: Fine-needle aspiration of the node shows squamous cell carcinoma. Which test on the tissue matters most next? A: p16 immunohistochemistry

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving > step 2: Imaging
statement: Axial contrast CT: a cystic left level II node (arrows) deep to the sternocleidomastoid, beside the internal jugular vein. Chengazi HU, Bhatt AA, Insights Imaging 2019 (PMC6377693), CC BY 4.0.

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving > step 2: Imaging
statement: CT neck with contrast: a 4.2 cm cystic left level II node. No other enlarged nodes.

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving > step 2: Imaging
statement: p16 is the surrogate for HPV: the HPV E7 protein inactivates pRb, which drives p16 up. p16 status decides which staging system you use and frames prognosis.

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving > step 3: Stage
statement: Axial MRI through the oropharynx: an asymmetric mass in one tonsillar region.

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving > step 3: Stage
statement: Scope and MRI: a 2.3 cm left tonsil mass that stays lateral; it does not reach the base of tongue or soft palate.

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving > step 3: Stage
statement: Biopsy: nonkeratinizing squamous cell carcinoma, p16 positive.

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving > step 3: Stage
statement: PET/CT: only the left tonsil and the single left level II node; no distant disease.

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving > step 3: Stage
statement: 2.3 cm is T2 (more than 2 and up to 4 cm).

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving > step 3: Stage
statement: In p16-positive disease, any ipsilateral nodes all 6 cm or less are cN1, no matter how many.

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving > step 4: Treatment
statement: HPV changes the prognosis, not the treatment.

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving > step 4: Treatment
statement: De-escalated doses are only given on trials.

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving > step 5: Trial
statement: Q: He read online that cetuximab is gentler than cisplatin and asks to swap. Which trials answered this question for HPV-positive oropharynx cancer? A: RTOG 1016 and De-ESCALaTE

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving > step 5: Trial
statement: In RTOG 1016 and De-ESCALaTE, cetuximab with RT gave worse survival and more recurrences than cisplatin, without meaningfully less toxicity.

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving > step 7: Side effects
statement: Oral mucositis during radiation for oropharyngeal cancer. Owosho AA et al., Dent J (Basel) 2023 (PMC10217705), CC BY 4.0.

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving > step 7: Side effects
statement: Mucositis peaks around weeks 4-6 and heals over the weeks after treatment.

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving > step 7: Side effects
statement: Dental evaluation and fluoride trays come before RT starts.

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear > step 2: Workup
statement: Q: Which set of tests best completes his workup? A: Nasopharyngoscopy with biopsy, MRI of the skull base and neck, plasma EBV DNA, and PET/CT

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear > step 2: Workup
statement: MRI is the modality of choice for the nasopharynx because skull base and perineural spread drive the T-stage.

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear > step 2: Workup
statement: Plasma EBV DNA and EBER testing on the biopsy are the nasopharynx-specific additions.

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear > step 2: Workup
statement: PET/CT checks nodes and distant disease, which matter in a cancer that presents with bulky nodes.

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear > step 3: Stage
statement: FDG PET/CT: avid tumor filling the nasopharynx on axial, sagittal, and coronal fused views.

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear > step 3: Stage
statement: Endoscopy: a mass filling the right fossa of Rosenmüller.

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear > step 3: Stage
statement: Biopsy: nonkeratinizing, undifferentiated carcinoma, EBER positive.

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear > step 3: Stage
statement: MRI: tumor extends into the right parapharyngeal space; skull base intact; no intracranial spread.

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear > step 3: Stage
statement: PET/CT: no distant disease.

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear > step 3: Stage
statement: Plasma EBV DNA: elevated.

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear > step 3: Stage
statement: Parapharyngeal spread is T2 (bony skull base would be T3; intracranial or cranial nerve involvement T4).

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear > step 6: Late effects
statement: Q: Besides dry mouth, which late effects will you watch for, given that the target sits under the skull base, near the ears, and he is getting cisplatin? A: Hearing loss (cisplatin plus dose to the cochlea, and lasting ear fluid), hypothyroidism from neck RT, temporal lobe injury, cranial nerve problems, trismus, and swallowing trouble.

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear > step 6: Late effects
statement: These are discussed before treatment and screened for afterward: audiograms, TSH checks, and a careful neuro and jaw exam at follow-up.

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear > step 7: Follow-up
statement: Q: Which blood test helps track his response and watch for relapse? A: Plasma EBV DNA

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear > step 7: Follow-up
statement: Plasma EBV DNA tracks the disease in nasopharyngeal carcinoma. A level that clears after treatment is reassuring, and a rising level suggests relapse.

section: Case 5: The Sore That Won't Heal > step 1: Exam
statement: Q: Biopsy shows invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Which imaging best measures the feature that drives T-stage at this site? A: MRI, to measure depth of invasion

section: Case 5: The Sore That Won't Heal > step 2: Imaging
statement: Axial contrast-enhanced T1 MRI of a left oral tongue cancer. J Korean Soc Radiol 2026 (PMC12883927), CC BY-NC 4.0.

section: Case 5: The Sore That Won't Heal > step 2: Imaging
statement: MRI: a 1.8 cm left lateral oral tongue tumor with a depth of invasion of about 7 mm, not crossing the midline.

section: Case 5: The Sore That Won't Heal > step 2: Imaging
statement: CT neck: no enlarged or necrotic nodes.

section: Case 5: The Sore That Won't Heal > step 2: Imaging
statement: CT chest: clear.

section: Case 5: The Sore That Won't Heal > step 2: Imaging
statement: The tumor is 2 cm or less, but DOI over 5 mm makes it T2 (DOI of 5 mm or less would be T1).

section: Case 5: The Sore That Won't Heal > step 3: Plan
statement: Q: What is the primary treatment? A: Partial glossectomy with negative margins plus an elective neck dissection

section: Case 5: The Sore That Won't Heal > step 3: Plan
statement: Her neck looks negative, but the neck is dissected anyway: the Tata Memorial trial showed better survival with an elective neck dissection than with waiting for a node to appear, especially when DOI is over about 3-4 mm.

section: Case 5: The Sore That Won't Heal > step 4: Pathology
statement: Left partial glossectomy and left neck dissection (levels I-III): 2.0 cm squamous cell carcinoma, DOI 8 mm, perineural invasion present, margins negative (closest 6 mm).

section: Case 5: The Sore That Won't Heal > step 4: Pathology
statement: Chemo is only added for a positive margin or extranodal extension (step 3), and she has neither.

section: Case 5: The Sore That Won't Heal > step 4: Pathology
statement: A single ipsilateral node of 3 cm or less without ENE is pN1.

section: Case 5: The Sore That Won't Heal > step 6: Trial
statement: Both trials asked whether adding cisplatin to postoperative RT helps high-risk patients.

section: Case 5: The Sore That Won't Heal > step 6: Trial
statement: Their pooled analysis found a consistent benefit only for ECE/ENE and positive margins, which is framework step 3.

section: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck > step 1: Scope
statement: Q: Which finding on this scope already makes the tumor at least T3? A: The fixed right vocal cord

section: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck > step 1: Scope
statement: Videoendoscopy of a right supraglottic tumor: swelling of the right false cord and aryepiglottic fold. Crosetti E et al., Front Oncol 2024 (PMC10847842), CC BY 4.0.

section: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck > step 1: Scope
statement: Laryngoscopy: a bulky right supraglottic mass involving the false cord and aryepiglottic fold and extending down to the glottis.

section: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck > step 1: Scope
statement: Biopsy: squamous cell carcinoma, p16 negative.

section: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck > step 2: Stage
statement: CT neck: tumor fills the right paraglottic space and the pre-epiglottic fat.

section: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck > step 2: Stage
statement: PET/CT: no distant disease.

section: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck > step 3: Key question
statement: A functional larynx goes to chemoradiation; a destroyed larynx (cartilage destruction, T4a, or a non-functional airway or swallow) goes to total laryngectomy.

section: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck > step 5: Trial
statement: VA Larynx came first: induction chemo then RT matched surgery for survival, and 64% kept their larynx.

section: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck > step 5: Trial
statement: Its main endpoint was laryngectomy-free survival, and overall survival was similar across arms.

section: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck > step 7: What if
statement: A different patient: axial contrast CT of an advanced laryngeal cancer destroying the cricoid and thyroid cartilages. Joshi VM et al., Indian J Radiol Imaging 2012 (PMC3624744), CC BY-NC-SA 3.0.

section: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck > step 7: What if
statement: Through the outer thyroid cartilage cortex is T4a, a destroyed larynx.

section: Case 7: Eight Months Later > step 1: Surveillance
statement: After treatment, CT and MRI often can't tell residual tumor from scar.

section: Case 7: Eight Months Later > step 2: Symptoms
statement: Hypothyroidism is common after neck radiation because the thyroid sits in the low neck field.

section: Case 7: Eight Months Later > step 2: Symptoms
statement: It usually shows up months to years after treatment, so TSH is checked regularly in follow-up and replaced with levothyroxine when low.

section: Case 7: Eight Months Later > step 3: Dry mouth
statement: Saliva loss from parotid dose can be permanent; IMRT reduces it by sparing the parotids.

section: Case 7: Eight Months Later > step 5: Complication
statement: Still biopsy anything that looks like a mass or a suspicious ulcer, because recurrence can mimic it.

section: Case 8: Can't Open Wide > step 1: Exam
statement: Q: He can only open his mouth about this far. What does new trismus suggest about a tumor in this region? A: Involvement of the pterygoid muscles and masticator space

section: Case 8: Can't Open Wide > step 1: Exam
statement: How trismus is measured: maximal mouth opening of about 6 mm with a ruler between the incisors (shown in a patient after head and neck radiation). Owosho AA et al., Dent J (Basel) 2023 (PMC10217705), CC BY 4.0.

section: Case 8: Can't Open Wide > step 1: Exam
statement: New trouble opening the mouth means the tumor has reached them, and masticator space invasion is T4b in the oral cavity.

section: Case 8: Can't Open Wide > step 2: Numb chin
statement: The marginal mandibular branch is motor (lip asymmetry), not sensory.

section: Case 8: Can't Open Wide > step 3: Stage
statement: Axial contrast CT: a retromolar trigone cancer eroding the right mandible. Jones W et al., Oral Oncol Rep 2025 (PMC12199806), CC BY-NC 4.0.

section: Case 8: Can't Open Wide > step 3: Stage
statement: CT: erosion through the cortex of the right mandible.

section: Case 8: Can't Open Wide > step 3: Stage
statement: PET/CT: no distant disease.

section: Case 8: Can't Open Wide > step 3: Stage
statement: Masticator space, pterygoid involvement, or skull base spread makes it T4b.

section: Case 8: Can't Open Wide > step 4: Imaging
statement: Q: Which of these is NOT an MRI sign of perineural spread? A: A cystic level II node

section: Case 8: Can't Open Wide > step 4: Imaging
statement: A cystic level II node is a classic HPV-positive oropharynx finding, not a perineural sign.

section: Case 8: Can't Open Wide > step 6: Target
statement: Perineural spread can carry tumor beyond what is visible, so the field follows the nerve.

section: Case 8: Can't Open Wide > step 7: Late risk
statement: Prevention: dental extractions before RT, lifelong fluoride, quitting tobacco, and daily jaw-stretching exercises to fight trismus.

section: Flashcard ov-70 (Treatment Planning)
statement: Q: What do the nested target volumes GTV, CTV, ITV, and PTV each add? A: GTV = visible tumor. CTV adds microscopic spread. ITV adds internal motion (e.g., breathing). PTV adds daily setup uncertainty.

section: Flashcard ov-74 (Treatment Planning)

section: Flashcard ov-88 (Radiation Modalities)

section: Flashcard ov-90 (Radiation Modalities)
statement: Q: Do protons automatically give better results than photons? A: No. Their Bragg peak removes exit dose, which may matter in selected cases (children, craniospinal RT, tumors next to critical structures). Drawbacks: range uncertainty and sensitivity to anatomic change.

section: Case 1: A Lump in the Shower
statement: A 27-year-old woman felt a smooth, rubbery lump in her left breast while showering. It moves easily under her fingers and doesn't hurt. She has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer.

section: Case 1: A Lump in the Shower > step 2: Ultrasound
statement: Q: Which feature, had it been present, would have made this mass suspicious for cancer? A: Taller than wide, with posterior acoustic shadowing

section: Case 1: A Lump in the Shower > step 2: Ultrasound
statement: Suspicious masses are hypoechoic, irregular or spiculated, taller than wide, and cast a posterior shadow.

section: Case 1: A Lump in the Shower > step 2: Ultrasound
statement: Reassuring masses are oval, circumscribed, wider than tall, and may show posterior enhancement.

section: Case 1: A Lump in the Shower > step 4: Diagnosis
statement: A fibroadenoma is a benign tumor and the most common breast mass in young women. There is no cancer to stage and no role for radiation.

section: Case 2: The Callback > step 1: Mammogram
statement: Q: The magnified views show fine, linear, branching (casting) calcifications over a 2.5 cm segment, BI-RADS 4C. What do calcifications like these most suggest? A: High-grade (comedo) DCIS

section: Case 2: The Callback > step 1: Mammogram
statement: Linear and casting calcifications suggest high-grade (comedo) DCIS; fine granular ones suggest lower-grade DCIS.

section: Case 2: The Callback > step 1: Mammogram
statement: DCIS shows up as calcifications alone in 50-75% of cases, and its true extent is usually larger than the calcifications.

section: Case 2: The Callback > step 5: Plan
statement: Nodes are not treated for DCIS.

section: Case 2: The Callback > step 5: Plan
statement: ER-positive DCIS can get endocrine therapy for risk reduction.

section: Case 3: The Grandmother's Question
statement: A 73-year-old woman with high blood pressure and arthritis has a new 1.3 cm mass in her left breast found on screening. She looks after her grandchildren and wants the least treatment that is still safe.

section: Case 3: The Grandmother's Question > step 1: Mammogram
statement: A spiculated mass is one of the three classic suspicious findings, with pleomorphic or linear calcifications and architectural distortion.

section: Case 3: The Grandmother's Question > step 2: Pathology
statement: HER2 1+ is negative.

section: Case 3: The Grandmother's Question > step 2: Pathology
statement: HR-positive/HER2-negative is the most common group, is often relatively indolent when low grade, and is treated with endocrine therapy.

section: Case 3: The Grandmother's Question > step 3: Systemic
statement: Q: Which systemic therapy is the backbone of her treatment? A: An aromatase inhibitor for 5-10 years

section: Case 3: The Grandmother's Question > step 3: Systemic
statement: Hormone receptor positive, HER2 negative disease is treated with endocrine therapy for 5-10 years: an aromatase inhibitor after menopause, tamoxifen before.

section: Case 4: The Left-Sided Plan > step 2: Sequencing
statement: Chemo is never given at the same time as breast RT. Endocrine therapy and anti-HER2 drugs, by contrast, can run during RT.

section: Case 4: The Left-Sided Plan > step 4: The heart
statement: Adding the internal mammary nodes would make heart sparing harder, not easier.

section: Case 5: Two of Three > step 2: Pathology
statement: 2 of 3 sentinel nodes positive (largest deposit 6 mm), no extranodal extension.

section: Case 2: Double Vision > step 2: Surgery?
statement: Q: It grew from 2.0 to 2.5 cm over 18 months and encases the cavernous carotid. Why not simply remove it? A: Cavernous sinus tumors encase the carotid and cranial nerves, so resection risks stroke and new nerve deficits and is usually incomplete

statement: Both give about 90-95% control at 5 years. The choice depends on size and distance from the optic apparatus.

section: Case 2: Double Vision > step 5: Side effects

statement: How can an endometrial cancer reach para-aortic nodes without pelvic nodes?

section: gyn-lymph
statement: Fundal lymphatics run with the ovarian (gonadal) vessels in the infundibulopelvic ligament straight to the para-aortic nodes.

statement: What is the nodal pathway for the vulva, and what is Cloquet's node?

section: gyn-lymph
statement: Superficial inguinal → deep femoral → external iliac (pelvic). Cloquet's node is the highest deep femoral node, under the inguinal ligament, the gateway to the pelvis.

section: gyn-lymph

section: Case 2: After the Surgery > step 1: Stage
statement: Confined to the cervix: IB1 is 2 cm or less, IB2 over 2 and up to 4 cm, IB3 over 4 cm. Parametrial invasion would be IIB.

statement: Q: Which criteria does her pathology meet? A: Sedlis (intermediate risk)

statement: Open radical hysterectomy and sentinel nodes: 3.2 cm squamous cell carcinoma, LVSI present, invasion into the middle third of the cervical stroma.

section: Case 2: After the Surgery > step 3: Pathology
statement: LVSI-positive with middle-third invasion and a tumor 2 cm or larger meets Sedlis.

section: Case 3: Bleeding After Intercourse > step 2: Stage
statement: Parametrial invasion not reaching the pelvic side wall is IIB.

section: Case 3: Bleeding After Intercourse > step 2: Stage
statement: Side wall involvement or hydronephrosis would be IIIB; pelvic nodes IIIC1; bladder or rectal mucosa IVA.

section: Case 4: A Node on PET > step 1: Stage
statement: Any pelvic node makes it IIIC1, whatever the size of the primary. The 'r' means radiology found it; 'p' means pathology. Para-aortic nodes would be IIIC2.

section: Case 4: A Node on PET > step 2: Surgery?
statement: If nodes are found during surgery, the hysterectomy is often abandoned in favor of chemoRT.

section: Case 4: A Node on PET > step 3: Plan
statement: Many add the para-aortic nodes when common iliac or multiple pelvic nodes are involved.

section: Case 4: A Node on PET > step 6: Late effect
statement: The ovaries receive a sterilizing dose in pelvic chemoRT.

section: Case 4: A Node on PET > step 6: Late effect
statement: In patients treated with surgery, ovarian transposition can preserve function; here it is too late, so plan for menopausal symptoms and bone health.

section: Case 6: The Node at L3 > step 1: Stage
statement: Para-aortic nodes are IIIC2, still regional and treated for cure. Supraclavicular nodes or organ metastases would be IVB.

section: Case 5: One Sentinel Node > step 1: Stage

section: Case 5: One Sentinel Node > step 2: MMR
statement: Q: What does the MMR-deficient result mean for her and her family? A: Screen for Lynch syndrome with germline testing; MMR-deficient tumors also respond well to immunotherapy

section: Case 5: One Sentinel Node > step 2: MMR
statement: Lynch syndrome raises the risk of colorectal, endometrial, and other cancers in her relatives. MMR deficiency predicts benefit from checkpoint inhibitors.

section: Case 5: One Sentinel Node > step 3: Adjuvant
statement: Node-positive endometrial cancer is chemo-led, with pelvic EBRT often added for pelvic and vaginal control.

section: Case 5: One Sentinel Node > step 5: Immunotherapy
statement: Q: Which systemic addition is especially helpful for her MMR-deficient tumor? A: A checkpoint inhibitor (dostarlimab or pembrolizumab) added to chemo

section: Case 5: One Sentinel Node > step 6: Dose

section: Case 7: An Itch That Became a Sore > step 1: Groins

section: Case 7: An Itch That Became a Sore > step 2: Stage

section: Case 7: An Itch That Became a Sore > step 2: Stage

section: Case 7: An Itch That Became a Sore > step 3: Adjuvant
statement: Two or more positive nodes, extracapsular extension, or a sentinel node metastasis over 2 mm call for groin and pelvic RT.

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics
statement: GYN anatomy comes down to three questions: which organ (and which part of it), what is next to it (the bladder, rectum, bowel, and the tissue beside the cervix), and where its lymph drains.

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Uterus and Cervix
statement: Picture the uterus as an upside-down pear sitting between the bladder and the rectum, usually tipped forward (anteverted) over the bladder.

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Uterus and Cervix
statement: From top to bottom: the fundus, the body (corpus), and the cervix, the narrow neck that pokes down into the vagina.

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Uterus and Cervix
statement: The wall has three layers: the endometrium (the lining), the myometrium (thick muscle), and the serosa (a thin peritoneal coat).

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Uterus and Cervix
statement: The cervical canal runs from the internal os (where it meets the uterine body) to the external os (its opening into the vagina).

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Uterus and Cervix
statement: The canal is lined by glandular (columnar) cells and the outer cervix by squamous cells.

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Uterus and Cervix
statement: That is why most cervical cancers are squamous and a minority are adenocarcinomas.

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Ligaments and Parametria
statement: The cervix is anchored in place by ligaments. They matter because tumor and lymph travel along them.

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Ligaments and Parametria
statement: Cardinal Ligament

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Ligaments and Parametria
statement: Runs from the cervix sideways to the pelvic side wall.

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Ligaments and Parametria
statement: The fatty tissue around it is the parametrium, which carries the uterine artery, the ureter, and lymphatics.

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Ligaments and Parametria
statement: Uterosacral Ligament

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Ligaments and Parametria
statement: Runs from the cervix back around the rectum to the sacrum. A lymphatic path to the presacral nodes.

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Ligaments and Parametria
statement: Broad Ligament

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Ligaments and Parametria
statement: A sheet of peritoneum draped over the uterus and tubes. Its infundibulopelvic part carries the ovarian vessels up toward the para-aortic region.

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Ligaments and Parametria
statement: Round Ligament

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Ligaments and Parametria
statement: Runs from the top corner of the uterus through the inguinal canal to the labia. A rare route to the groin nodes.

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Ligaments and Parametria
statement: Cervical cancer grows sideways into the parametria, toward the side wall.

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Ligaments and Parametria
statement: The ureter passes under the uterine artery about 2 cm lateral to the cervix ("water under the bridge").

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Vagina
statement: A muscular tube about 7 to 9 cm long running up and back from the introitus to the cervix.

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Vagina
statement: The easiest way to remember it is in thirds, because each third has different neighbors and drains to a different place.

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Vagina
statement: Part | Neighbors | Lymph drains to

statement: Middle third | Bladder and urethra in front, rectum behind | Pelvic nodes

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Vagina
statement: Lower third | Urethra in front, anal canal and perineal body behind | Groin (inguinofemoral) nodes, like the vulva

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Vagina
statement: The posterior wall sits on the rectum (the rectovaginal septum) and also drains to presacral nodes.

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Vagina
statement: After a hysterectomy, the top of the vagina is sewn closed as the vaginal cuff.

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Vulva
statement: The external genitalia: the mons pubis, labia majora (outer, hair-bearing skin) and labia minora, the clitoris, the urethral meatus, the vaginal introitus, the Bartholin glands, and the perineal body between the vagina and anus.

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Vulva
statement: Most vulvar cancers are squamous cancers of the labia majora. Think of the vulva as skin: it drains like skin, to the groins.

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Vulva
statement: The midline matters.

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Vulva
statement: A lesion well off to one side (2 cm or more from the midline) drains mainly to one groin.

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Vulva
statement: The urethra, vagina, and anus all sit within a few centimeters, so even modest tumors can reach them.

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Vulva
statement: The ureter runs through the parametrium, under the uterine artery about 2 cm lateral to the cervix.

section: Anatomy & Lymphatics > The Vulva
statement: Tumor spreading sideways squeezes it, urine backs up, and the kidney swells (hydronephrosis).

statement: Not oropharynx. The anterior 2/3 of the tongue belongs to the oral cavity and is treated with surgery first.

section: Case 1: The Spot on the Tongue
statement: A 57-year-old man who smokes a pack a day and drinks four beers a night is sent by his dentist for a painless white patch on the left side of his tongue. It has been there for about 3 months.

section: Case 1: The Spot on the Tongue > step 1: Exam
statement: The lesion on exam: a white plaque on the left lateral tongue. Coronation Dental Specialty Group, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

section: Case 1: The Spot on the Tongue > step 1: Exam
statement: Thrush wipes off; this does not.

section: Case 1: The Spot on the Tongue > step 1: Exam
statement: The lateral tongue is the most common site of oral cavity cancer, and his tobacco and alcohol use raise the stakes.

section: Case 1: The Spot on the Tongue > step 2: Risk factors
statement: Oral cavity cancer is the classic tobacco, alcohol, and betel nut cancer.

section: Case 1: The Spot on the Tongue > step 3: Biopsy
statement: A radiation oncologist only meets this patient if an invasive cancer develops.

section: Case 1: The Spot on the Tongue > step 4: Counseling
statement: Q: He asks how likely a white patch like this is to turn into cancer. Using the figure from the epidemiology reading, what is the risk over about 10 years? A: About 1-20%

section: Case 1: The Spot on the Tongue > step 4: Counseling
statement: Leukoplakia carries roughly a 1-20% risk of malignant transformation over 10 years, and dysplasia (especially severe dysplasia) sits at the higher end.

section: Case 2: The Raspy Voice
statement: A 66-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history has had a hoarse voice for 4 months. He has no trouble swallowing or breathing and has not noticed any neck lumps.

section: Case 2: The Raspy Voice > step 1: Localize
statement: Q: Which part of the larynx best explains persistent hoarseness as the first and only symptom? A: Glottis (true vocal cords)

section: Case 2: The Raspy Voice > step 1: Localize
statement: Even a small tumor on a true cord changes the voice, so glottic cancer tends to be caught early.

section: Case 2: The Raspy Voice > step 2: Scope
statement: The left cord still moves, but less than the right.

section: Case 2: The Raspy Voice > step 2: Scope
statement: He has both.

section: Case 2: The Raspy Voice > step 4: Treatment
statement: Early glottic cancer is treated with radiation to the larynx alone, or with larynx-preserving surgery (transoral or partial laryngectomy).

section: Case 2: The Raspy Voice > step 5: Nodal levels
statement: The supraglottis, in contrast, drains richly to both sides of the neck, so early supraglottic cancer gets bilateral levels II-IV.

section: Case 2: The Raspy Voice > step 6: Counseling
statement: Also: no treatment breaks, because tumor repopulation means delays cost cure.

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving
statement: A 49-year-old man who has never smoked noticed a painless lump on the left side of his neck while shaving. It has been there for 6 weeks and did not go away after a course of antibiotics.

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving > step 1: Exam
statement: The primary is often small or hidden in the tonsil or base of tongue.

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving > step 1: Exam
statement: An adult neck mass that persists after antibiotics is cancer until proven otherwise.

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving > step 2: Imaging
statement: EBER testing is the move when the story points to the nasopharynx.

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving > step 6: Nodal levels
statement: Q: His tonsil primary is well lateralized. Which elective neck coverage fits? A: Left neck only: levels II-IV and VII (retropharyngeal), plus Ib and V because level II is involved

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving > step 6: Nodal levels
statement: A well-lateralized tonsil cancer without base of tongue or soft palate involvement is the classic exception that allows one-sided neck treatment.

section: Case 3: The Lump Found While Shaving > step 6: Nodal levels
statement: Any pharyngeal primary adds level VII, and an involved level adds its neighbors (involved II: cover Ib and V) at an elective dose.

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear
statement: A 44-year-old man who grew up in Guangdong, China, has felt fullness in his right ear for 3 months. His doctor found fluid behind the right eardrum and treated it twice without improvement. He now has lumps on both sides of his neck.

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear > step 1: Localize
statement: Q: An adult with fluid behind one eardrum and new neck nodes. Where is the primary most likely? A: Nasopharynx (fossa of Rosenmüller)

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear > step 1: Localize
statement: One-sided serous otitis media in an adult means eustachian tube blockage until proven otherwise; scope the nasopharynx.

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear > step 1: Localize
statement: Add his geography and neck nodes and this is the classic nasopharyngeal carcinoma story.

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear > step 3: Stage
statement: A right retropharyngeal node, bilateral level II nodes, and a right level V node, the largest 3.5 cm, all above the cricoid.

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear > step 3: Stage
statement: Cranial nerve exam normal.

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear > step 4: Treatment
statement: The nasopharynx is not treated with surgery because the skull base is in the way; surgery is saved for salvage.

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear > step 5: Nodal levels
statement: Q: Which nodal coverage is right? A: Both sides, levels II-V, plus the retropharyngeal nodes (VII)

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear > step 5: Nodal levels
statement: Three rules stack here: any pharyngeal primary adds level VII, the nasopharynx is the one site that routinely adds level V, and a midline primary means both sides of the neck.

section: Case 4: The Ear That Won't Clear > step 5: Nodal levels
statement: The neck is always treated in nasopharynx cancer, even when it looks negative.

section: Case 5: The Sore That Won't Heal
statement: A 62-year-old woman who smoked for 40 years has had a painful sore on the side of her tongue for 2 months that she blamed on a sharp tooth. Filing the tooth down didn't help, and the pain now spreads to her left ear.

section: Case 5: The Sore That Won't Heal > step 1: Exam
statement: An ulcerated lesion on the lateral border of the tongue. Dikkisherpa5, Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

section: Case 5: The Sore That Won't Heal > step 1: Exam
statement: The oral cavity is the only head and neck site where depth of invasion (DOI) is built into the T-stage.

section: Case 5: The Sore That Won't Heal > step 2: Imaging
statement: A small but deep tumor can outstage a larger, superficial one.

section: Case 5: The Sore That Won't Heal > step 2: Imaging
statement: The DOI cutoffs to remember are 5 mm and 10 mm.

section: Case 5: The Sore That Won't Heal > step 3: Plan
statement: Oral cavity cancer is surgery first.

section: Case 5: The Sore That Won't Heal > step 4: Pathology
statement: 1 of 24 nodes positive (left level II, 1.4 cm), no extranodal extension.

section: Case 5: The Sore That Won't Heal > step 7: Before RT
statement: Teeth pulled after RT heal poorly in irradiated bone.

section: Case 5: The Sore That Won't Heal > step 7: Before RT
statement: Speech and swallow evaluation, nutrition support, and smoking cessation round out the pre-treatment visits.

section: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck
statement: A 64-year-old man with a 60 pack-year smoking history and heavy alcohol use has 3 months of sore throat, pain when swallowing, and a muffled voice. He has lost 15 pounds.

section: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck > step 1: Scope
statement: The right vocal cord is fixed.

section: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck > step 1: Scope
statement: His airway is adequate and he can still swallow liquids.

section: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck > step 1: Scope
statement: The neuro and scope exam is part of staging.

section: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck > step 2: Stage
statement: The outer cortex of the thyroid cartilage is intact; no spread outside the larynx.

section: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck > step 2: Stage
statement: Nodes: a 2.5 cm right level II node and a 2 cm left level III node, no ENE.

section: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck > step 3: Key question
statement: Q: Which question decides between total laryngectomy and organ preservation? A: Does the larynx still work, or is it destroyed?

section: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck > step 3: Key question
statement: Larynx cancer treatment is about organ preservation.

section: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck > step 4: Treatment
statement: Induction chemo followed by RT or chemoRT, or total laryngectomy with neck dissection, are the alternatives.

section: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck > step 6: Nodal levels
statement: Q: Which neck coverage fits? A: Both sides, levels II-IV, with elective coverage of the levels next to the involved nodes

section: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck > step 6: Nodal levels
statement: This is the supraglottis, not the glottis: it drains richly to both sides of the neck.

section: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck > step 6: Nodal levels
statement: Involved nodes get full dose, and the levels next to them (for the right level II node, Ib and V) get an elective dose.

section: Case 6: Food Getting Stuck > step 7: What if
statement: Organ preservation works poorly here and often leaves a larynx that doesn't function, so surgery comes first; chemoRT is only for select patients who decline surgery.

section: Case 7: Eight Months Later > step 3: Dry mouth
statement: Q: His mouth is still very dry, and he carries a water bottle everywhere. Which statement is most accurate? A: Dry mouth is often a lasting late effect of dose to the parotid glands, and it raises his risk of cavities

section: Case 7: Eight Months Later > step 3: Dry mouth
statement: Less saliva means more cavities, which is one reason fluoride trays are lifelong.

section: Case 7: Eight Months Later > step 4: Dental
statement: This is why bad teeth are extracted before RT, and why the dental team stays involved for life.

section: Case 7: Eight Months Later > step 5: Complication
statement: Exposed necrotic bone where a lower left molar was lost, in a patient treated with radiation for left tonsil cancer. Owosho AA et al., Dent J (Basel) 2023 (PMC10217705), CC BY 4.0.

section: Case 7: Eight Months Later > step 6: Red flag
statement: Most recurrences happen within the first 2 years.

section: Case 8: Can't Open Wide
statement: A 59-year-old man who smokes and chews tobacco has 3 months of right jaw pain. Over the last month he can barely open his mouth, and the right side of his lower lip and chin have gone numb.

section: Case 8: Can't Open Wide > step 1: Exam
statement: The pterygoid muscles open and close the jaw.

section: Case 8: Can't Open Wide > step 2: Numb chin
statement: The inferior alveolar nerve runs through the mandible and exits as the mental nerve to supply the lower lip and chin.

section: Case 8: Can't Open Wide > step 3: Stage
statement: Exam: an ulcerated mass behind the last right lower molar (retromolar trigone).

section: Case 8: Can't Open Wide > step 3: Stage
statement: Nodes: a 2.5 cm right level Ib node and a 2 cm right level II node, no ENE.

section: Case 8: Can't Open Wide > step 4: Imaging
statement: Nerve thickening, foraminal widening, loss of perineural fat, and abnormal nerve enhancement are the signs to know.

section: Case 8: Can't Open Wide > step 5: Treatment
statement: RT alone is for patients who can't take chemo.

section: Case 8: Can't Open Wide > step 6: Target
statement: Lateralized oral cavity tumors can sometimes be treated on one side, but bulky, deep disease like this often gets both sides.

section: Case 8: Can't Open Wide > step 7: Late risk
statement: High dose to a mandible that the tumor has already eroded, plus poor dentition and tobacco, means a high ORN risk.

section: Flashcard hn-10 (Anatomy)
statement: Early glottic nodal risk is only about 2-5%. The supraglottis drains richly to both sides of the neck, so supraglottic cancer gets bilateral neck coverage.

section: Flashcard hn-10 (Anatomy)
statement: Q: Which laryngeal compartment has almost no lymphatics, and what does that mean for treatment? A: The glottis (true vocal cords). Early glottic cancer is treated without covering the neck.

section: Flashcard hn-11 (Lymph Nodes)
statement: Two bones and one cartilage divide the jugular chain.

section: Flashcard hn-11 (Lymph Nodes)
statement: Q: Which landmarks divide neck levels II, III, and IV? A: The hyoid separates II from III, and the cricoid separates III from IV (the clavicle is the bottom of IV).

section: Flashcard hn-12 (Lymph Nodes)
statement: Other add-ons: subglottic extension → level VI; lower lip, anterior tongue, or anterior floor of mouth → level Ia.

section: Flashcard hn-12 (Lymph Nodes)
statement: Q: Which head and neck site routinely adds level V (posterior triangle) to the elective neck? A: Nasopharynx

section: Flashcard hn-17 (Workup & Staging)
statement: A small but deep tumor can outstage a larger, superficial one.

section: Flashcard hn-17 (Workup & Staging)
statement: Q: What feature is built into the T stage of oral cavity cancer but no other head and neck site? A: Depth of invasion (DOI), with cutoffs at 5 mm and 10 mm

section: Flashcard hn-2 (Epidemiology & Risk Factors)
statement: Q: What are the classic risk factors for oral cavity cancer? A: Tobacco, alcohol, and betel nut (areca) chewing

section: Flashcard hn-20 (Imaging)
statement: Q: What imaging features make a cervical lymph node suspicious for cancer? A: Short axis >10 mm, loss of the fatty hilum, or cystic/necrotic change

section: Flashcard hn-30 (Treatment Paradigms)
statement: The skull base makes resection impractical. The neck, including level V and retropharyngeal nodes, is always treated.

section: Flashcard hn-30 (Treatment Paradigms)
statement: Q: How is nasopharyngeal carcinoma treated, and what role does surgery play? A: Radiation: RT alone for T1N0 and chemoradiation (often after induction chemo) for nearly everyone else. Surgery is only for salvage.

section: Flashcard hn-34 (Anatomy)
statement: Tonsil and base of tongue refer pain through CN IX (Jacobson's nerve); larynx and hypopharynx through CN X (Arnold's nerve).

section: Flashcard hn-36 (Anatomy)
statement: Scope the nasopharynx. Other NPC presentations: neck mass (most common), nasal obstruction or epistaxis, and cranial nerve palsies.

section: Flashcard hn-37 (Anatomy)
statement: The neuro exam is part of staging in the nasopharynx.

section: Flashcard hn-42 (Workup & Staging)
statement: Nasopharynx T stage also follows where the tumor spread (soft tissue → bone → intracranial/cranial nerves), not its size.

section: Flashcard hn-51 (Lymph Nodes)
statement: Levels II-IV are covered for almost every H&N site, usually on both sides.

section: Flashcard hn-51 (Lymph Nodes)
statement: Q: Which neck level is the most commonly involved in head and neck cancer? A: Level II (upper jugular)

section: Flashcard hn-52 (Lymph Nodes)
statement: Retropharyngeal nodes are the first echelon for nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

section: Flashcard hn-53 (Lymph Nodes)
statement: Midline or near-midline primaries (base of tongue, soft palate, pharyngeal wall, supraglottis, nasopharynx) get both sides.

section: Flashcard hn-53 (Lymph Nodes)
statement: Q: When can only one side of the neck be treated in head and neck cancer? A: For a well-lateralized primary that drains to one side, classically a tonsil cancer without base of tongue or soft palate involvement

section: Flashcard hn-55 (Imaging)
statement: Don't call a cystic neck node in an adult a benign branchial cleft cyst until this is excluded.

section: Flashcard hn-58 (Treatment Paradigms)
statement: Managed with pain control, nutrition support (sometimes a feeding tube), and oral care. Taste loss and thick saliva are also common.

section: Flashcard hn-6 (Epidemiology & Risk Factors)
statement: Salt-preserved fish is the classic dietary risk factor.

section: Flashcard hn-7 (Anatomy)
statement: Same organ, two different diseases with different staging and treatment.

section: Flashcard hn-8 (Anatomy)
statement: The other two oropharynx subsites are the soft palate and posterior pharyngeal wall. Base of tongue primaries can be tiny and hidden behind a big neck node.

section: Anatomy > Oral Cavity

section: Anatomy > Oral Cavity
statement: Gingiva / alveolar ridge | Sits right on bone, so mandible invasion happens early.

section: Anatomy > Oral Cavity

section: Anatomy > Oral Cavity
statement: The circumvallate papillae split the tongue: in front is oral tongue (oral cavity), behind is base of tongue (oropharynx).

section: Anatomy > Oropharynx
statement: Base of Tongue

section: Anatomy > Oropharynx
statement: Posterior 1/3 of the tongue. Tumors can be small and hidden and still present with a big neck node.

section: Anatomy > Oropharynx
statement: The roof. Midline, so both sides of the neck are at risk.

section: Anatomy > Oropharynx
statement: Posterior Pharyngeal Wall

section: Anatomy > Oropharynx
statement: Midline too. Drains to the retropharyngeal nodes.

section: Anatomy > Oropharynx
statement: Circumvallate papillae and anterior tonsillar pillars

section: Anatomy > Oropharynx
statement: Soft palate (above it is the nasopharynx)

section: Anatomy > Oropharynx
statement: Vallecula and tip of the epiglottis (below it are the larynx and hypopharynx)

section: Anatomy > Oropharynx
statement: Tonsillar fossae and pillars; beyond them the parapharyngeal space and pterygoid muscles

section: Anatomy > Oropharynx
statement: Posterior pharyngeal wall and prevertebral muscles

section: Anatomy > Nerves & Presentations: Oropharynx
statement: Referred otalgia via CN IX.

section: Anatomy > Nerves & Presentations: Oropharynx
statement: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the tonsil and base of tongue and also the middle ear.

section: Anatomy > Nerves & Presentations: Oropharynx

section: Anatomy > Nasopharynx

section: Anatomy > Nasopharynx
statement: C1-C2 and the prevertebral muscles

section: Anatomy > Nasopharynx

section: Anatomy > Nasopharynx
statement: Eustachian tube opening, torus tubarius, and the fossa of Rosenmüller

section: Anatomy > Nerves & Presentations: Nasopharynx

section: Flashcard ov-1 (Radiation 101)
statement: Systemic therapy treats cancer cells (including micrometastases) anywhere in the body. Most patients are planned at a multidisciplinary tumor board.

section: Flashcard ov-1 (Radiation 101)
statement: Q: Of the three cancer treatment specialties, which give local therapy and which gives systemic therapy? A: Local: surgical oncology and radiation oncology. Systemic: medical oncology (chemo, immunotherapy, targeted and hormone therapy).

section: Flashcard ov-101 (Treatment Planning)
statement: Q: When is a hotspot in a radiation plan acceptable, and when is it a problem? A: A small hotspot inside the tumor is usually fine; one inside an organ at risk (e.g., the spinal cord) is not.

section: Flashcard ov-103 (The Rad Onc Consult)
statement: Q: What is consolidative radiation? A: RT given after another treatment modality, usually chemotherapy, to improve control of the disease that remains (e.g., residual bulky lymphoma).

section: Flashcard ov-104 (Treatment Planning)
statement: Q: Why is not a DVH enough on its own to judge a plan? A: It shows how much dose each structure receives, not where; hotspots and coverage gaps must be checked on the isodose lines slice by slice.

section: Flashcard ov-105 (How to Give a Presentation)
statement: Q: When you build a Rad Onc HPI, what question decides whether a detail belongs in it? A: Would this fact change the diagnosis, the stage, the treatment, or radiation safety? If not, it probably does not belong.

section: Flashcard ov-106 (How to Give a Presentation)
statement: Then name what is still open, for example whether a complete response might allow organ preservation.

section: Flashcard ov-2 (The Rad Onc Consult)
statement: Always ask what the intent of this specific treatment is; one patient's plan can include both.

section: Flashcard ov-31 (How Radiation Works)
statement: Prostate and breast cancers are exceptions with low α/β.

section: Flashcard ov-31 (How Radiation Works)
statement: Q: Which tissues have a high α/β ratio and which have a low one? A: High (~10): early-responding tissues (skin, mucosa, marrow) and most tumors. Low (~3): late-responding tissues (spinal cord, lung, kidney, liver, bladder).

section: Flashcard ov-33 (Treatment Planning)
statement: A teaching simplification: many organs behave partly both ways, and the actual limits are site- and protocol-specific.

section: Flashcard ov-45 (How Radiation Works)
statement: A fifth R, intrinsic radiosensitivity, is sometimes added.

section: Flashcard ov-45 (How Radiation Works)
statement: Q: What are the four R's of radiobiology that explain why we fractionate? A: Repair, reoxygenation, repopulation, and redistribution

section: Flashcard ov-47 (How Radiation Works)
statement: Bulky or necrotic tumors are harder to control partly for this reason.

section: Flashcard ov-47 (How Radiation Works)
statement: High-LET radiation (neutrons, alpha particles) damages DNA directly and depends much less on oxygen, so its oxygen enhancement ratio falls toward 1.

section: Flashcard ov-48 (How Radiation Works)
statement: Q: Why can treatment breaks make radiation less effective? A: Surviving tumor cells keep dividing (repopulation) during gaps in treatment.

section: Flashcard ov-54 (How Radiation Works)
statement: Single-strand breaks are easily repaired off the intact opposite strand; double-strand breaks are what lead to lethal chromosome damage.

section: Flashcard ov-54 (How Radiation Works)
statement: Q: What is the main way radiation kills cancer cells? A: DNA damage, especially double-strand breaks, which kill the cell when it tries to divide

section: Flashcard ov-55 (How Radiation Works)
statement: Oxygen "fixes" this free-radical damage, which is why oxygen matters.

section: Flashcard ov-56 (Radiation Modalities)
statement: Q: Why are deep tumors treated with several photon beams or arcs instead of one? A: Photons pass through the tumor and keep going (exit dose), so overlapping beams build the highest dose at the tumor while spreading the lower dose across normal tissue.

section: Flashcard ov-59 (Radiation Modalities)
statement: The depth is set by the beam energy.

section: Flashcard ov-59 (Radiation Modalities)
statement: Several energies are combined into a spread-out Bragg peak (SOBP) to cover the full tumor thickness.

section: Flashcard ov-6 (The Rad Onc Consult)
statement: Other "do not forget" items for a new patient: fertility counseling before gonadal exposure, a pregnancy test when relevant, genetic counseling when a hereditary syndrome is suspected, and performance status.

section: Flashcard ov-61 (Radiation Modalities)
statement: Q: What do the multileaf collimators (MLCs) in a LINAC do? A: Their thin metal leaves move to shape the beam to the target and block normal tissue.

section: Flashcard ov-70 (Treatment Planning)
statement: Not every case uses every layer.

section: Flashcard ov-76 (Treatment Planning)
statement: A good plan covers the target while sparing everything else.

section: Flashcard ov-76 (Treatment Planning)
statement: Q: In plan review, what is the difference between coverage and conformity? A: Coverage asks whether the whole target (including its edges) gets the prescribed dose; conformity asks how tightly the high-dose region hugs the target.

section: Flashcard ov-77 (Treatment Planning)
statement: It lets you check every target and organ at risk against its limits without scrolling through every slice.

section: Flashcard ov-77 (Treatment Planning)
statement: Q: What does a dose-volume histogram (DVH) show? A: What percentage of a structure's volume receives at least each dose

section: Case 1: The Drive Is Two Hours > step 1: Imaging
statement: Q: His bone scan is shown. What kind of metastases does prostate cancer usually cause, and why does the bone scan show them so well? A: Blastic (bone-forming), because the tracer collects where new bone is being made

section: Case 1: The Drive Is Two Hours > step 1: Imaging
statement: Whole-body Tc-99m bone scans from other patients: normal (left), multiple metastases (middle), and a superscan (right). Qureshi AM et al., World J Nucl Med 2017 (PMC5314659), CC BY-NC-SA.

section: Case 1: The Drive Is Two Hours > step 1: Imaging
statement: Prostate cancer is the classic blastic metastasis.

section: Case 1: The Drive Is Two Hours > step 1: Imaging
statement: Bone scan tracer is taken up where bone is being formed, so blastic lesions light up.

section: Case 1: The Drive Is Two Hours > step 1: Imaging
statement: Purely lytic lesions (myeloma especially) can be missed.

section: Case 1: The Drive Is Two Hours > step 2: Before you plan
statement: An uncomplicated bone metastasis means no impending fracture, no cord or nerve compression, and no prior surgery to the site.

section: Case 1: The Drive Is Two Hours > step 2: Before you plan
statement: Night pain that steroids help is biologic pain from the tumor, which responds well to RT.

section: Case 1: The Drive Is Two Hours > step 3: Fractionation
statement: One visit matters for a man with limited performance status who lives far away.

section: Case 1: The Drive Is Two Hours > step 6: Three months later
statement: Strontium and samarium relieve pain only.

section: Case 10: What Are You Hoping For? > step 2: First conversation
statement: Q: What is the most useful first question in the room? A: "What are you hoping this treatment will do for you?"

section: Case 2: Tripping on the Stairs
statement: A 63-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer calls with 4 weeks of mid-back pain. Over the last 2 days she has been tripping on the stairs and her legs feel heavy.

section: Case 2: Tripping on the Stairs > step 1: First orders
statement: Image the whole spine because many patients have more than one level.

section: Case 2: Tripping on the Stairs > step 2: Grade
statement: Grade 2 still shows some CSF around a compressed cord; grade 1 touches the thecal sac without deforming the cord.

section: Case 2: Tripping on the Stairs > step 4: Surgery or RT
statement: Breast cancer is relatively radiosensitive, so if her spine were stable or she could not have surgery, urgent radiation alone would be a reasonable choice (NOMS).

section: Case 2: Tripping on the Stairs > step 4: Surgery or RT
statement: Steroids are a bridge, not a treatment, and systemic therapy works too slowly for a cord at risk.

section: Case 5: It Hurts to Stand
statement: A 56-year-old woman with ER-positive breast cancer, metastatic to bone only, has 3 weeks of left thigh pain that is much worse when she bears weight.

section: Case 5: It Hurts to Stand > step 1: Red flag
statement: Q: Which feature of her pain worries you most? A: It is worse with weight bearing

section: Case 5: It Hurts to Stand > step 1: Red flag
statement: Functional pain (pain with weight bearing) in a long bone suggests impending fracture. Keep her off the leg until orthopedics weighs in.

section: Case 5: It Hurts to Stand > step 2: Score it
statement: Q: X-rays show a lytic lesion in the femoral shaft involving more than two-thirds of the bone's width. Calculate the Mirels score. A: Lower limb 2 + functional pain 3 + lytic 3 + more than 2/3 of the width 3 = 11.

section: Case 5: It Hurts to Stand > step 2: Score it
statement: Site (upper 1, lower 2, peritrochanteric 3), pain (mild 1, moderate 2, functional 3), lesion (blastic 1, mixed 2, lytic 3), width (under 1/3: 1, 1/3-2/3: 2, over 2/3: 3).

section: Case 5: It Hurts to Stand > step 3: Next step
statement: Q: What is the next step? A: Orthopedic referral for prophylactic fixation, then postoperative RT

section: Case 5: It Hurts to Stand > step 3: Next step
statement: A Mirels score of 9 or more means high fracture risk. Fixing the bone before it breaks is much easier than fixing a fracture.

section: Case 6: A Tight Collar
statement: A 61-year-old man who smokes has 2 weeks of facial swelling, a feeling that his shirt collars are too tight, and dilated veins over his upper chest. He is breathing comfortably and is alert.

section: Case 6: A Tight Collar > step 4: Fast relief
statement: A stent relieves symptoms within hours to a day or two; radiation takes 1-2 weeks or more.

section: Case 3: Lumps in the Palm
statement: A 67-year-old retired carpenter has firm, slowly growing nodules in his right palm at the base of the ring finger for 8 months. They're tender when he grips tools.

section: Case 3: Lumps in the Palm > step 1: Diagnosis
statement: Q: Exam shows two palmar nodules and a short cord, and he can lay his hand flat on the table. What is the diagnosis? A: Early Dupuytren disease

section: Case 3: Lumps in the Palm > step 1: Diagnosis
statement: A negative tabletop test means no significant contracture yet.

section: Case 3: Lumps in the Palm > step 2: Role of RT
statement: Q: Why is radiation reasonable now and not later? A: RT works on the proliferating fibroblasts of early disease, slowing progression; it can't straighten a finger once a mature cord has formed

section: Case 3: Lumps in the Palm > step 2: Role of RT
statement: The key word for Dupuytren radiation is early.

section: Case 3: Lumps in the Palm > step 3: Regimen
statement: The same approach treats Ledderhose disease of the sole.

section: Case 3: Lumps in the Palm > step 4: Counseling
statement: Benign radiation is offered after weighing age, site, and alternatives.

section: Case 3: Lumps in the Palm > step 5: Five years later
statement: A fixed contracture is beyond what radiation can fix.

section: Case 7: Brushing Her Teeth
statement: A 71-year-old woman has 2 years of sudden, electric shock-like pain in her right cheek and jaw lasting a few seconds. It is triggered by brushing her teeth, chewing, and cold wind.

section: Case 7: Brushing Her Teeth > step 1: Diagnosis
statement: Q: Her neurologic exam is normal between attacks. What is the diagnosis? A: Trigeminal neuralgia

section: Case 7: Brushing Her Teeth > step 3: First line
statement: Carbamazepine (or oxcarbazepine) controls pain in most patients at first.

section: Case 7: Brushing Her Teeth > step 4: Procedure
statement: Q: Carbamazepine now makes her dizzy and confused, and she takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. Which procedure fits her best? A: Stereotactic radiosurgery

section: Case 7: Brushing Her Teeth > step 5: Dose and target
statement: The dose is prescribed to the center of the tiny target, not to its edge.

section: Case 7: Brushing Her Teeth > step 6: Counseling
statement: Outcomes are reported with the BNI pain score.

section: Case 4: Before the Second Hip
statement: A 69-year-old man is scheduled for a right total hip replacement next week. Two years ago, after his left hip replacement, bone grew in the soft tissue around the joint and he lost much of his range of motion.

section: Case 4: Before the Second Hip > step 1: Diagnosis
statement: Q: What happened after his first operation? A: Heterotopic ossification

section: Case 4: Before the Second Hip > step 1: Diagnosis
statement: Heterotopic ossification is bone forming in soft tissue, most often around the hip after arthroplasty or acetabular fracture surgery.

section: Case 4: Before the Second Hip > step 2: Risk
statement: Q: What is the strongest risk factor for heterotopic ossification after his second hip replacement? A: Prior heterotopic ossification

section: Case 4: Before the Second Hip > step 2: Risk
statement: Prior HO is the strongest predictor. Others: ankylosing spondylitis, DISH, hypertrophic osteoarthritis, and male sex.

section: Case 4: Before the Second Hip > step 3: Regimen and timing
statement: Radiation kills the precursor cells before they become bone-forming cells, which happens in the first few days.

section: Case 4: Before the Second Hip > step 3: Regimen and timing
statement: Once bone has formed, radiation can't remove it.

section: Case 4: Before the Second Hip > step 4: Technique
statement: Q: His new prosthesis will be uncemented, with a porous coating. Which statement about the plan is most accurate? A: Cover the soft tissue around the joint where bone would form; whether to shield the porous components varies by institution

section: Case 4: Before the Second Hip > step 4: Technique
statement: Radiation prevents bone from forming; it cannot remove bone that is already there.

section: Case 4: Before the Second Hip > step 5: Alternative
statement: Q: What is the main non-radiation alternative? A: NSAIDs such as indomethacin

section: Case 8: A Seizure at Work > step 2: Grade
statement: Q: Angiography shows a 2.4 cm AVM in the left thalamus with deep venous drainage. What is the Spetzler-Martin grade? A: Size under 3 cm (1) + eloquent location (1) + deep venous drainage (1) = grade III.

section: Case 8: A Seizure at Work > step 2: Grade
statement: Grades I-II usually go to surgery. Small, deep, or eloquent AVMs are the classic radiosurgery cases.

section: Case 8: A Seizure at Work > step 3: Treatment
statement: Q: It has already bled. Which treatment fits best? A: Stereotactic radiosurgery

section: Case 8: A Seizure at Work > step 4: Dose
statement: Higher doses close more AVMs but cause more injury to surrounding brain, especially in eloquent areas.

section: Case 8: A Seizure at Work > step 5: Latency
statement: The vessels close slowly.

section: Case 8: A Seizure at Work > step 5: Latency
statement: Obliteration is confirmed by angiography, usually around 3 years.

section: Case 9: Nothing Hurts Yet > step 1: Which lesions
statement: Q: He has a 3.5 cm lesion in the left acetabulum, a lesion in the posterior elements at T12-L1, and several small rib lesions. Which lesions put him at high risk for a skeletal-related event? A: The bulky acetabular lesion and the junctional T12-L1 lesion

section: Case 9: Nothing Hurts Yet > step 1: Which lesions
statement: Bulky lesions (2 cm or more), hip, shoulder, or sacroiliac joint involvement, junctional spine levels, and posterior vertebral involvement mark high-risk lesions.

section: Case 9: Nothing Hurts Yet > step 2: Trial
statement: Gillespie (JCO 2024): in 78 patients with more than 5 metastases, skeletal-related events at 1 year fell from 29% to 1.6% of lesions.

section: Case 9: Nothing Hurts Yet > step 3: Plan
statement: Q: What is reasonable now? A: Discuss prophylactic RT to the acetabular and T12-L1 lesions, continuing systemic therapy

section: Case 9: Nothing Hurts Yet > step 3: Plan
statement: Small, low-risk rib lesions are left alone, and systemic therapy continues.
